title: Abnormal health-check results: push through or see a doctor
situation: You tell your manager about the results. There is no fuss, and Priya covers for you. Follow-up tests show the nodule is benign and the extra beats are linked to late nights and caffeine. The doctor gives you a plan and stresses sleep. You are relieved, and you also take it as your body's first warning. Back at work, you have to decide how hard to push.

options.text: Reset how you work: fixed hours, with the high-intensity work spread out
Nothing serious showed up, so you fall back into late-night sprints

title: Funding and listing rumours — bet on the share options?
situation: Word is the company is raising money or heading for a listing. People talk as if the share options will make them rich, and they tell you to 'hang on a few more years for the options — don't leave'. The rumours are hard to pin down and a payout looks a long way off. You are not sure you should hang a career decision on it.

options.text: Count the share options as a possible bonus and decide on the fundamentals of the job
Turn down a better offer in front of you and stay put for options that have been over-promised
Ignore the options entirely, count only cash, and leave as soon as something better comes up

title: A new manager is hired in, and you start again on trust
situation: The heavy flattery gets a polite response, but they have already clocked it. What they care about is people who deliver. Colleagues find it embarrassing too. Grovelling has not got you a solid relationship or anyone’s respect.

options.text: Change tack: let your ability and delivery rebuild how they see you
Keep spending your energy on flattery

title: The company goes all-in on a new bet and sidelines your work
situation: You put your hand up for the new work, start with what you can already do, and contribute quickly on the engineering basics. The people running it notice that you learn fast and can be relied on, and they are willing to give you more. Competition is fierce, though. To stay, you still have to produce something real.

options.text: Put your head down, make a real contribution and establish yourself on the new work
Get in, then coast because you don't want to keep grafting

title: Whether to share the method you have kept to yourself
situation: The post takes off. Lauren uses the write-up to improve the system, and your manager asks you to standardise it across the team.

options.text: Lead training for the whole group and step up as the technical expert
Worry about being replaced and start holding things back again

title: The colleague who buys coffee is collecting favours for a lead vote
situation: Harvey brings the team coffees from Pret every day and never takes money. You notice a notebook: “Favours ledger: Chris +2, Ethan +1…” The team is about to pick an acting lead, and Harvey is standing. Today he hands you a larger coffee: “Put in a word for me at the review tonight?”

options.text: Refuse to campaign. In the review, stick to the facts
Agree to talk him up, in return for later support
Warn your manager privately that someone is trading favours for support
Start buying coffees yourself and join the favours game

title: Late-night work messages and the manager's reaction
situation: Colleague Tara posts "today's progress" and "tomorrow's plan" in the channel every night at 11pm. Your manager, Chris, is often first to react. You are never online at that hour. In the weekly meeting Chris said "we need to respond promptly". Tonight Tara @channels a question about an API field.

options.text: Reply at once to look professional
Reply in the morning and spell out your working hours
Suggest to your manager privately that important items go by email
Copy Tara and start sending late-night updates yourself

title: A leaver asks you to keep work files off the company systems
situation: One evening Felix, who is leaving for a competitor, sends you a link to 8GB of files in cloud storage: “Three years of project scripts and client-contact notes. I wiped the company drive — keep this for me, and don’t upload it here.” Some of the files are scanned client contracts marked Internal. You know his leaver agreement says he must not take business data with him.

options.text: Refuse the files and tell him to use the proper handover
Take the link without opening it, and plan to delete it later
Take it and report it to Information Security

title: Named on a department award you did not work on
situation: Aurora wins. You are named at the awards. Three months later internal audit picks the pack for a spot check and asks you to describe exactly what you contributed to the platform.

options.text: Admit you were not part of the core work
Invent a contribution that matches your manager’s story

title: Lunch with the team, or keep the break to yourself
situation: Your delivery stays solid, but in a review Warren says you “don’t really know the team’s pain points”. Missing lunch has left you out of the loop.

options.text: Start joining lunch occasionally, specifically to catch up
Keep skipping the café, and book 1:1s with the people who matter

title: Seated with a senior leader at the Christmas party
situation: The praise comes across as oily. They smile politely and change the subject, and people at the table wince on your behalf. Laying it on this thick has had the opposite effect to the one you wanted.

options.text: Stop, and go back to ordinary, honest conversation
Keep finding new ways to compliment them

title: Forced ranking: scoring a colleague who is also a friend
situation: It is time for year-end 360 reviews, and the department uses a forced A/B/C split (20% / 60% / 20%). You have to rate Ethan, a friend who has babysat for you and trains with you. But he carried about 30% of the blame for a Lynx Wallet incident this year, and his output has been ordinary. An A for him means taking a slot from someone else. A C could hit his annual bonus.

options.text: Give him a fair B and write clear points for improvement
Give him an A, taking the slot from a colleague you know less well
Give him a C, because the incident has to show in the rating
Recuse yourself and ask your manager to have someone else rate Ethan

title: Pitching against a cheaper rival
situation: You walk through a solid technical design and a cost-of-ownership model that explains the price. The technical panellists nod along. Procurement still stares at the number: “You’re well above the other bid. How do we sell this to our leadership?”

options.text: Offer staged payments plus a measurable ROI model procurement can repeat upstairs
Keep talking technology and dodge the pricing question

title: Who owns your side-project algorithm?
situation: In your own time, and without directly using company resources, you have built an algorithm related to the company's work. It could be a product in its own right. Your contract says inventions connected to the business belong to the company. That clause alone does not settle it. Ownership depends on your duties, how the work was made, and what the contract can actually do. Being named as inventor

options.text: Go along with the company filing, but ask to be named as inventor with a personal licence to use it
Argue it is a personal invention with no direct tie to the business, and refuse a company filing

title: A milestone briefing for the execs
situation: You got lost in the process. The execs checked their watches several times, then cut in: 'What's the conclusion? Is there a risk?' You did not get to the point in the time you had, and the briefing went down badly.

options.text: Stop at once and give the conclusion, the risk and your request in three sentences
Keep reading the pack at your own pace

title: A colleague accidentally posts internal architecture online
situation: Security investigates and judges the leak containable. Your colleague is hurt to find out you reported it, and tells the people they are close to that you shopped them. Helping them take the post down and then reporting the accident was the normal security step.

options.text: Explain to the team how the report worked, and that security rules are not optional
Say nothing, and trust that time will show you made the right call

title: The office war over windows and heating
situation: You set out what each of them needs and suggest a fixed middle temperature, a small screen to keep the draught off Maya, and a desk fan for Hugh. Both feel looked after, and most of the heat goes out of the row. To make it happen, someone has to ask facilities for the extras.

options.text: Take the lead with facilities and get the extras in
You had the idea. They can chase it themselves

title: A database migration window clashes with peak trading
situation: Product accepts the delay. Architecture reminds you that 5.7 support ends at the end of the month.

options.text: Commit to a fixed 72-hour migration plan straight after peak trading
Cite safety and push it back another month

title: The office war over windows and heating
situation: You kept your head down. The two of them dug in further and ended up asking your manager to referee. Your manager frowns: 'You can't sort out something this small?' Everyone who could have stepped in and didn't, you included, now looks as if it is nothing to do with them. The atmosphere is awkward for days.

options.text: Step in late with a middle option so both of them have a way out
Stay out of it. It's still not your problem

title: A project you wanted going to someone else
situation: Owen agrees on the surface (“let's do it together”), but in updates outside the team they mostly put their own name on the work. Your manager praises Owen in the channel for “pushing the new direction hard”. You need to decide what to do next.

options.text: Clarify your actual contribution and what you want with your manager
Drop it and go back to focusing on the live project

title: The lunchtime badminton league and your body's limits
situation: The sports club is running a badminton league. The captain wants you in: your game and fitness are both decent. An old neck and shoulder injury has flared up, though, and the project is in a sprint. You want to be part of it, but you know your body has limits.

options.text: Sign up, and say upfront that the old injury limits how hard you can play
Sit the matches out and help behind the scenes with the draw, the kit and the cheering
Grit your teeth and go all in, to prove you can take it

title: A milestone briefing for the execs
situation: At the company's quarterly leadership review, you have to report on a milestone for a project you own. The execs are short of time and only want conclusions and risks. They have no interest in process. There is still an unresolved risk on the project, and progress is only 'broadly on track'. You have ten minutes.

options.text: Lead with the conclusion: key results first, then the risk and the plan to deal with it
Give only the good news: hide the risk and stick to highlights throughout
Walk through the process in detail, still not reaching the point ten minutes in

title: Admitting you are not coping, and asking for help
situation: After three months of a high-pressure project you are not sleeping, you cannot concentrate, and your temper is going. Last week you lost it with a colleague in the morning meeting over a design disagreement, and you have been kicking yourself since. The Employee Assistance Programme counsellor suggests a short period of leave. The project is at a critical milestone, and your manager hints that any

options.text: Follow the sick-leave procedure, and privately agree the support and return-to-work plan you need
Grit it out, try exercise and meditation, and deal with it after the project

title: Lunch with the team, or keep the break to yourself
situation: At noon the team usually heads to a café near the office to swap project gossip and guesses about what your manager is thinking. It is where people pick up the unofficial news. For the past few months you have eaten at your desk or gone for a walk instead. You get a real break and are sharper in the afternoon. Colleagues have started calling you the lone wolf. At last week’s offsite your manager s

options.text: Switch to lunching with colleagues at least three days a week
Keep skipping the café, and let a strong afternoon prove the point
Compromise: Tuesdays and Thursdays with the team, the break to yourself the rest

title: You notice a remote colleague is often offline
situation: While working remotely you notice a colleague you get on with is often offline in working hours, with Slack showing them away for more than three hours, yet their output has not obviously dropped. The team is meant to be outcomes-led, and you also know they are looking after a sick relative.

options.text: Check in privately: ask how they are, and whether they need help or a change to the arrangement
Leave it and trust that managing by outcomes will sort it out

title: Your company is acquired and the culture flips
situation: You cling to the old culture and keep resisting. The new leadership sees you as hard to integrate and unwilling to change. You miss out on what the deal could have offered and become a candidate for the next round of cuts.

options.text: Face facts, let go of the old ways, and get behind the new organisation
Keep looking backwards and resisting to the end

title: Peer review finds a serious bug in a friend's code
situation: Craig, a colleague you get on well with, has an SQL injection risk in his merge request. He messages privately: “Merge it for now — I'll buy dinner tonight and fix it after.”

options.text: Block the review and require a fix before merge
Merge it and help him fix it this evening
Comment but do not block

title: Christmas at home clashing with the on-call rota
situation: You are on the Christmas on-call rota, which clashes with going home for the break. It is the only time in the year your older relatives really get together.

options.text: Negotiate a fair swap with a colleague, and offer to cover them later
Quietly accept the shift and skip going home
Skip the on-call shift without warning anyone

title: Your partner's job offer in another city: live apart, stay, or rethink
situation: You talk your partner out of the offer. In the short term your career is untouched, but they often show regret, the atmosphere at home turns strained and you feel guilty. Six months later they are clearly low, and the sacrifice starts to damage the relationship. How do you make amends?

options.text: Make it up to them: make room for their next opportunity and take on more at home
Take their sacrifice for granted and keep putting your own career first

title: Client makes an inappropriate joke at dinner
situation: You stop the remark without a scene and bring the talk back to the work. The client looks uncomfortable. Chloe is glad someone drew a line. Nobody asks her to repair the relationship. That job belongs to the account lead.

options.text: Leave the client relationship with the account lead, and ask Chloe only what support she wants
Decide you were in the right, and make no effort to repair it

title: How blunt to be in a code-review comment
situation: Priya, who has just joined, opens her first merge request. The design is clearly wrong. You can write in the review that this will blow up in production, or you can ask questions until she sees it herself. The team's culture is fairly direct, and HR has just started talking about psychological safety.

options.text: Name the problem directly and mark it as must-fix
Use questions so she spots the issue herself
Approve it, and explain on Slack afterwards

title: A colleague keeps helping themselves to your snacks
situation: You keep a few snacks in your drawer. Colleague Mia "just grabs a handful" every day, never brings her own, and has never returned the favour. Today she grins, "Yours are the best." It isn't much, but it is starting to grate.

options.text: Joke: "Bring some next time and we can swap", and leave it there
Keep sharing, because you don't like to say anything
Lock the snacks away and stop sharing, without explaining

title: Christmas-party rehearsals eating your evenings
situation: The department is putting on an optional group number at the Christmas party. The organiser has booked evening rehearsals — an hour or two after work, most weekdays, for a fortnight. Your actual job is busy and your personal plans are a mess. It is voluntary. A lot of people are going, and your manager will notice who does.

options.text: Show up, and work with the organiser on a tighter rehearsal plan so the day job still fits
Attend every rehearsal and let the day job pile up
Skip a lot of sessions — “I’m not here to dance when there’s real work”

title: Stuck on the ladder: move into management or go deeper?
situation: You are a senior engineer, and you have been stuck at the same level for years. Technical roles above you are scarce, but management posts, oddly, are open. You can keep grinding on the specialist track and wait for one of the few expert roles, or move sideways into management and take a different route up.

options.text: Look hard at how far each path goes, how well you fit and how the company promotes, before you decide
Push into management, which you neither enjoy nor are good at, just for the title and the pay
Do neither: stay put and complain that the company won't give you a chance

title: A live demo blows up in front of the client
situation: You are at the client's offices demonstrating a new feature. At the key checkout step the system throws an error and the page freezes. Their decision-makers sit opposite you, waiting to see it work. You know the demo environment is flaky, but the room has already gone cold.

options.text: Say plainly it's a demo-environment glitch, and switch to a fallback or recording to show the core value
Keep hitting refresh as it gets messier, without switching plan
In a panic, say it is a problem on the client's network

title: Mentoring a graduate who breaks things
situation: You have been mentoring Sam for barely two weeks when they skip your code review and merge lightly tested code into the pre-production branch. Staging is down all night and several neighbouring teams are blocked. At the next morning's standup your manager asks, stony-faced, 'Who is going to answer for this incident?' Sam stares at the floor. Everyone looks at you.

options.text: Take the main responsibility and say your oversight as mentor failed
Say in the room that the whole fault is Sam's

title: Desk politics in the new office
situation: The department is moving to a new office. Quiet window desks are scarce. Facilities has told teams to sort it out among themselves. Your work needs deep focus and noise easily distracts you, but you also don't want to be known as the person who grabs the good seats.

options.text: Propose open rules for allocation: the type of work, how often people collaborate, and a rotation
Quietly get a good desk through people you know, and avoid a public row
Don't compete at all, and take whatever desk you are randomly given

title: Company-wide AI tools, and the fear of being replaced
situation: The company is loudly rolling out AI coding and automation tools, wants everyone using them, and has said that 'the same work will be done with fewer people'. A lot of the day-to-day coding and boilerplate you own is exactly what AI does best. In the kitchen the talk is uneasy: 'Will the next round of cuts be us?' How do you respond?

options.text: Lean in: learn the AI tools well and use them to get more done
Play along in public but resist in private, sure it will never replace a real engineer
Spiral: spend your energy on redundancy rumours and looking for a safe spot

title: Lunch with the team, or keep the break to yourself
situation: At your third lunch you overhear people discussing who will get places on next quarter’s flagship project. Someone floats your name. Someone else says “we never see them.” You need to decide how often to keep going.

options.text: Keep lunching with the team every day
Drop back to Tuesdays and Thursdays once you have the key information

title: The company tries to keep you after you look elsewhere
situation: You think hard about why you wanted out. Was it money, growth, or a clash with how your manager works? Once that is clear, the question is whether this package fixes the thing you care about. Your manager is sincere and willing to listen.

options.text: Tell them what is really bothering you, agree a fix, then stay with a clear head
Feel too awkward to be honest, take the rise and leave the real problem unsolved

title: Whether to invest in a CI automation suite
situation: Your team still lacks a proper automated-test CI pipeline. Every release depends on senior engineers manually reviewing critical paths. Your manager wants you to lead the platform work. Headcount has just doubled from five to ten. New joiners' PRs have piled up, review pressure has spiked, and releases are starting to slip. Building a CI suite from scratch, with mocks, load tests and coverage gate

options.text: Spend two weeks building a full CI automation suite
Keep manual review and let new joiners follow the existing process

title: Neck pain with a deadline — whether to keep the physio appointment
situation: A stretch of late nights has left your neck aching and your right hand tingling. Physio is booked for tomorrow afternoon, which is also when a delivery checkpoint falls.

options.text: Keep the physio appointment and shift delivery by half a day
Move the appointment to the weekend and push through delivery first
Stick on a heat patch, tough it out, and leave physio for later

title: The new manager from outside wants you to inform on the team
situation: The manager hired from outside wants a quick picture of the team and takes you aside: 'You've been here. Tell me how people really are and who has issues. I'll remember you for it.' It could be a chance to be useful. It could also be a trap that makes you the informant.

options.text: Give a fair picture of the team and the work, without informing on anyone or running them down
Embellish complaints about colleagues to please the new manager
Refuse outright and brusquely, even to give a normal briefing

title: Do you say the code was AI-generated?
situation: You used an AI assistant to generate the core of a complex algorithm, edited it, and opened a pull request. The team has no rule on whether AI contributions need to be flagged. In review a colleague admires how clever the code is — and you realise they have no idea a model wrote the first draft.

options.text: Note in the PR that it was AI-assisted, and explain what you changed
Say nothing extra, and let it read as ordinary engineering

title: How intensely to mentor a new intern
situation: An intern, Alex, joined your team this week and, under company policy, is automatically assigned to you as mentor. The first two weeks matter most for onboarding. Alex is sharp but has no domain background and will need a lot of questions answered to get up to speed. Intensive mentoring (an hour of 1:1 a day, reviewing all their code, bringing them into every relevant meeting) would make them inde

options.text: Mentor intensively so they can work independently within two weeks
Keep a light touch, let them explore, and stay focused on your own work

title: Do you say the code was AI-generated?
situation: Later the team finds bugs nobody had spotted in AI-generated code elsewhere, and starts checking which changes were labelled. Your pull request is dug out of the history.

options.text: Go to your manager, admit you did not label it, and say you should have thought it through
Wait to be asked, then stress that there was no clear rule at the time

title: Telling the client the project will be late
situation: An upstream dependency has failed on a project you own. You now know you will be a week late, and the original delivery date is three days away. The client cares a lot about this one and has even put their own name behind it internally. You need to decide how to tell them.

options.text: Tell them at once, with a cause analysis, a recovery plan and a new timetable
Wait until delivery day in case you still make it
Report 'on time', then quietly work late and try to catch up

title: Whistleblowing on your manager's fake numbers
situation: You stumble on it: your manager has been systematically inflating project numbers in reports to senior leaders, and those numbers are feeding important company decisions. You have solid evidence. Reporting would mean a break with your line manager and an uncertain future. Staying silent could make you look like a party to the fraud, and that could come out at any time. What do you do first?

options.text: Secure the evidence and report carefully through compliance or internal audit
Speak to your manager privately and give them a chance to put it right
Protect yourself: pretend you did not see it, and keep your distance

title: A new manager is hired in, and you start again on trust
situation: You resist, and you keep talking about the last manager. The new one notices you are not cooperating and gives the important work to people who will go along with the changes. You have pushed yourself to the edge of the new team.

options.text: Drop the prejudice, adapt, and win trust back by delivering
Keep resisting and work against them

title: A database migration window clashes with peak trading
situation: At 03:40 on Sunday, replica lag spikes after cutover. Twenty hours remain before peak trading.

options.text: Roll back immediately, following the playbook
Stay up all night fixing it, without rolling back

title: A security hole that would be expensive to fix
situation: The release slips two weeks. Sales complain about lost deals. At the exec meeting the CEO asks whether a medium-severity issue is worth several million pounds of revenue. The CISO backs you in the meeting, then tells you privately that they held the line this time but want a more balanced answer from you next time.

options.text: Start a shift-left process, so similar issues are found much earlier
Soften your stance, and promise to be more 'pragmatic' in balancing security against the business

title: A promotion without a pay rise
situation: Your manager wants to talk about a 'promotion': a bigger title and a heavier workload, with the pay 'held for now — we'll look at it next year'. It is a better title with no rise: more prestige, more work, same money. The question is whether you take it, and on what terms.

options.text: Weigh what the title is actually worth, and whether it paves the way for a rise, before you negotiate
Get swept up by the title and take the lot without a second thought
Take the missing rise as an insult, refuse on the spot, and leave a sharp remark hanging

title: A toxic team culture: stay or leave?
situation: The VP hears about the letter. In an all-hands they say, without naming names, that anyone who cannot handle tough competition is free to leave. HR then sits you down. The CEO hired this VP personally, the company is fully behind the change, and are you willing to 'get with the programme'?

options.text: Stand your ground, and ask HR to open a formal investigation into the culture
Go along with a transfer for now, and start looking for jobs elsewhere

title: You bring an outside offer back to negotiate pay
situation: You have a real offer from another company, paying more. You are not set on leaving, and would prefer to use it as leverage for the rise you think you are owed here. Bringing an offer into a pay conversation can help or hurt you, depending on how you use it.

options.text: Be straight: you want to stay, here is what the market pays, and would they review your pay
Use the offer as an ultimatum: “Match this number or I go today”
Inflate the offer and quote your manager a much higher number

title: An internal transfer into a new area opens up
situation: The company has opened internal transfers. You can apply to join a team in a more promising new area. The chance is rare, but you would have to learn a lot from scratch and give up the advantage of work you already know well. What do you do?

options.text: Weigh your interest and transferable skills, then apply, ready to learn from scratch
Cling to your familiar role and skip the application
Apply on a rush of enthusiasm, without thinking through whether you can close the gap

title: Load-test results clash with what product expected
situation: Your manager supports a one-week slip. The client is mildly unhappy.

options.text: Work late and optimise to 80% of target capacity
Keep the delay

title: Choosing a stack for a new module
situation: You need to pick a stack for a new module. You could write the team's mature stack in your sleep, and it would almost certainly deliver on time. There is also a more modern framework with an active community that fits better in the long term. But neither you nor the team has used it in production, so expect pitfalls and an uncertain first release. The module is not on the critical path and the tim

options.text: Adopt the new framework and use this low-risk module to build experience
Stick with the mature stack and put reliable delivery first

title: Caffeine dependence and a broken sleep pattern
situation: Caffeine carries you for a while and you get the work done. Then you keep nodding off during the day and cannot sleep at all at night.

options.text: Finally cut out caffeine and get back to regular sleeping hours
Increase the dose and keep pushing

title: A new colleague with no sense of privacy
situation: Lou has just joined and is over-familiar from the start. Within days she has asked whether you own or rent, whether you are seeing anyone and how you get on with your manager. At lunch she also presses you on 'who on the team doesn't get on'. She means no harm and just doesn't seem to know where the line is, but the questions make you uncomfortable, and people nearby look awkward too.

options.text: Laugh it off and gently draw a line: 'Let's not go there. Talk about something else?'
Be blunt: 'That's private. Please don't ask'
Answer each question, not wanting to embarrass a new colleague

title: A collaborator shifts the blame in a meeting
situation: You and Chloe share delivery on a client project. In the weekly meeting the client complains about repeated API changes and thin test coverage. Chloe speaks first: “The API design was mainly theirs. I worked to the version they gave me. Testing was held up on their team too.” In fact the changes came from the client changing their mind three times, and you emailed several times for a test environm

options.text: Walk through the timeline and the email trail, and set out who owned what
Take some of the blame for now to steady the client, and leave Chloe for later
Hit back in the room: Chloe did not provide the integration environment on time
Stay silent and ask your manager to unpick it

title: A promotion without a pay rise
situation: The title goes to your head and you take everything on. The work doubles and the pay does not move. 'We'll look at it next year' stays a vague promise. You become known as capable, compliant and cheap, which weakens your hand when you do try to talk about money.

options.text: Reopen the conversation, using what you have already delivered in the new role as leverage
Keep grafting for no extra money and never bring up pay

title: Load-test results clash with what product expected
situation: The load test you ran shows the system can only take 60% of the expected QPS. The product owner insists the last demo was fine, so your method must be wrong. The go-live deadline does not move.

options.text: Invite product to review the scripts and scenarios with you
Stand by the numbers and ask to cut scope or slip the date
Tweak the test parameters until they 'pass', as product asked

title: Forced ranking: scoring a colleague who is also a friend
situation: Ethan’s bonus is in the normal range. Privately he says he understands. In calibration your manager uses your comments and asks him to write up the incident.

options.text: Help Ethan rework the write-up and keep the friendship
Keep your distance and stay strictly professional

title: Telling the client the project will be late
situation: The gamble failed, and you only told them on delivery day that it would be late. The client is furious: 'Why didn't you say? I can't explain this upstairs.' They want an explanation from the company. Your manager is pulled in.

options.text: Apologise in person at once, present a detailed recovery plan, and fix how you communicate
Explain why you were a victim of this too

title: Grey-area items on a travel expense claim
situation: You have just finished a week on a client site and are putting the expenses together. A few items sit in a grey area: 1) coffees you bought the client as a gift (no VAT receipt, only a till slip); 2) a late dinner you ordered for yourself after overtime (policy covers a 'working meal'; late dinners are not spelled out); 3) the taxi to the airport diverted to pick up a colleague travelling with you

options.text: Claim only the flights and hotels, which are clearly within policy, and drop every grey item
Claim as usual, taking colleagues' advice that 'everyone does this, it's fine'

title: A collaborator shifts the blame in a meeting
situation: The emails show the client and your manager exactly how the changes came about. Chloe looks grim. Afterwards your manager tells you and Chloe to “sort it between yourselves”. The client wants a joint improvement plan this week.

options.text: Draft a joint improvement plan, copy your manager, and invite Chloe to co-author it
Write only your own part and make clear where it ends

title: A colleague accidentally posts internal architecture online
situation: Browsing GitHub, you find that a colleague has posted an architecture diagram of an internal system in a public technical thread. Names have been removed, but anyone who knows the company would recognise it. It is clearly an accident: they were in a hurry to get help with a hard problem. Report it, and they may face disciplinary action. Warn them privately, and you may later be treated as having k

options.text: Help them take the post down, then report the accidental disclosure to security and say it was a mistake
Message them privately to take it down now, on the understanding that it goes no further

title: The lunchtime badminton league and your body's limits
situation: You play a run of hard games and win a key point. By evening your shoulder is really sore, and the next day even typing hurts.

options.text: Get it looked at, and ask the captain to change the rest of the plan
Say nothing and keep carrying both the job and the matches

title: Mentoring an intern as a first taste of management
situation: Your manager asks you to mentor a new intern. It will split your attention between teaching, checking in and covering for them, but it is also your first chance to try managing someone. How do you handle it?

options.text: Mentor them properly: plan, give feedback, and treat it as practice for leading people
Treat it as a distraction from your own work, phone it in and leave them to it
Use them as free labour: odd jobs only, no real teaching

title: Mentoring a graduate who breaks things
situation: The department has taken on a new batch of interns. Your manager gives you Sam, who has the flashiest university and the biggest ego, and hints that mentoring is an unofficial requirement for a top rating this year. You hear Sam nearly caused trouble in another team by merging unreviewed code, and most of the old hands have kept their distance. Do you take on the mentor role?

options.text: Take it on and set out clearly how the mentoring will work
Decline, citing your current workload

title: Invited to shadow a senior planning meeting
situation: As part of your development plan, the CTO invites you to shadow the quarterly executive strategy meeting. In the room you hear sensitive discussion about other departments, including possible restructuring and redundancies in a friend's team. The CTO makes clear it is strictly confidential. Afterwards your friend asks: 'I heard the exec meeting talked about an architecture change. What do you know

options.text: Keep it confidential. Tell them you cannot discuss anything from the meeting
Hint they have reason to pay attention, without specifics, and suggest they talk to their own manager

title: Forced ranking: scoring a colleague who is also a friend
situation: The colleague who lost the slot raises it with HR. HR look at the evidence and ask whether you rated him as a favour.

options.text: Admit the rating was too generous
Insist Ethan deserved an A

title: A restrictive covenant on the way out: take the pay or keep your options
situation: You sign without a close read and leave smoothly. Three months later a solicitor's letter arrives. The old employer says your new company is caught by the clause and asks you to stop. Whether the clause applies, and whether it can be enforced, is now in dispute. Your signature did not settle either question.

options.text: Stay calm, gather evidence, get professional help, and deal with the dispute by the rules
Panic, let them lead, and rush into a costly settlement

title: Should you work seriously on management and communication skills?
situation: Your technical work is strong, but communication, coordination, and dealing with senior people have always been the weak spots. Whether you stay on the engineering path or move into management, those skills matter more every year. Do you put real effort into closing the gap?

options.text: Treat soft skills as core skills too: study them and practise them deliberately
Dismiss them: 'the tech is what counts — the rest is fluff'
Say you will work on them, then never practise and keep your head in the code

title: A job spec from the big tech firm you have always wanted to join
situation: You come across a role that closely matches yours at a company you have always wanted to work for. Reading the spec, you feel envious and a bit anxious, because you are not there yet. What do you do with that feeling?

options.text: Use the spec as a yardstick and close the gaps in your current role until you could get it
Spend the days daydreaming about leaving, refreshing job boards, and letting the day job drift
Envy it and do nothing, telling yourself you would never get there anyway

title: Training a model on customer conversations: where is the line?
situation: The MVP is only middling, but Product uses its numbers to argue for wider use of customer data. Then a user asks on social media how an AI seemed to know about their conversation, and a small PR row breaks out. Comms piles in and wants engineering to prove there was no misuse.

options.text: Pull together the technical records, show the training data was kept separate from the MVP, and recommend starting full compliance now
Back the comms line, lean on the word 'anonymised', and play the risk down

title: One umbrella, a downpour, and Jordan at going-home time
situation: A release ran late and you are finally leaving. Rain is hammering the glass and the Met Office has an amber warning out. In your drawer is a single folding umbrella you picked up from a hotel on a previous trip. Jordan, a teammate, has just stood up too, with no umbrella, and is staring towards the lobby. They live two stops from you on the same line. Cabs are a forty-minute wait. You need to deci

options.text: Offer to share the umbrella and walk to the station together
Lend Jordan the umbrella and make a dash through the rain for a cab
Suggest sharing a cab and splitting the fare
Say the umbrella only covers one, so you will each make your own way

title: Escape room: your manager is slowing you down, a quiet colleague is flying
situation: Company escape room: The 1948 Files. Chris, your manager, insists on directing and is all over the place, retrying the same wrong codes. Quinn, usually quiet in testing, has just solved three puzzles in a row. Fifteen minutes left, one lock from the exit, and Chris is about to guess again.

options.text: Ask Quinn to take the lock, and tell Chris: “You keep the big picture”
Say outright that Chris’s approach is wrong
Follow Chris’s guesses so he is not made to look small

title: You notice promotions going to the people who play politics
situation: The CTO sees your talk at a tech conference and moves you into architecture, bypassing Chris's reporting line.

options.text: Take the move
Stay on the Lynx team

title: The new manager's first team meeting: make an impression?
situation: The manager hired from outside is holding their first team meeting, and this is when they start to size everyone up. You wonder whether to push yourself forward and make a good first impression.

options.text: Come prepared and give a clear, professional update on your work and thinking, without hogging the floor
Talk over people, overstate your role, and put colleagues down to make yourself look good
Keep your head down and say nothing all meeting, terrified of saying the wrong thing

title: Your partner's job offer in another city: live apart, stay, or rethink
situation: Your partner has a strong job offer in another city that could define their career, and taking it would mean living there. You are growing fast at your current company, and your programmes and network are here. The options are living apart, one of you giving way, or making a new plan together. Which way do you lean first?

options.text: Talk it through, back your partner and look into an internal move or remote working from their city
Keep things as they are: live apart, each build a career, and travel to see each other
Ask your partner to turn the offer down and stay for the household

title: Where personal use of work kit stops
situation: The company issues a high-spec workstation and a 4K display. Policy allows 'limited personal use' without saying exactly where the limit is. You have started using the work kit for a personal open-source project that does not compete with the business, and at weekends it soaks up a fair amount of compute. A colleague spots weekend commits from the office IP and jokes, 'So the company is sponsoring

options.text: Stop using work kit for the personal project immediately, and move it onto your own machines
Ask your manager and compliance whether the current use sits inside policy, and get it in writing

title: An undeclared relationship that looks like a conflict of interest
situation: HR opens an investigation and confirms the relationship from other sources. The manager is asked to declare it, denies it, then traces the original report back to you. They start telling the team someone 'went behind their back'. The atmosphere turns suspicious.

options.text: If confronted, own it and explain you raised a conflict of interest and meant nothing personal by it
Stay anonymous and carry on as normal in the team

title: Team morale is on the floor — should you step up?
situation: After the turmoil, the team is scattered and morale is low. Nobody has much energy for the work, and the gloom is spreading. You are not the manager, but your attitude still rubs off on the people around you.

options.text: Keep up your own pace, and privately give nearby colleagues some encouragement and a calmer view of things
Join the gloom, pile into the complaining, and make the pessimism louder
Treat it as none of your business, look after yourself, and ignore the team's mood

title: Empty your savings for a deposit, or keep cash in case work goes wrong
situation: You buy a reasonably priced place, keep six months of emergency cash, and the mortgage is manageable. You feel steadier, and at work you can make longer-term choices. Then the company offers a high-risk, high-reward crunch programme. Success would speed up promotion, and failure could drag down six months of performance ratings.

options.text: With a cash buffer behind you, take the high-reward programme and go for it
Play it safe, take steady work, and pay the mortgage down slowly

title: Colleagues invite you on a self-funded conference trip
situation: A few colleagues are planning to go to a tech conference in Singapore over the October half-term, with a couple of visits to friendly companies on the side. Most of it is self-funded. They are keen for you to come and say the trip will change how you see the work. You have a mortgage, and you are not sure the trip will lead to anything.

options.text: Sign up, but set a budget cap and learning goals first
Stay at home: follow it online and write it up yourself
Dither and leave the message unanswered

title: Dismissed in a team meeting as "just engineering work"
situation: You do not push back in the meeting. Afterwards you take a few colleagues for coffee and spell out the project's value and their part in it, and morale lifts. Your manager does not raise it again, and does not correct the remark in public either. You need to decide whether to take the point further.

options.text: Use the next meeting's pre-read to put business value in a summary your manager will see
Keep encouraging colleagues privately and do not raise it with your manager again

title: Who owns your side-project algorithm?
situation: Legal opens a file. They go through a year of your time records and commits, trying to show a technical link to a project you owned. Meanwhile your promotion review is paused because of the unresolved IP dispute.

options.text: Get independent advice from a solicitor who deals with employee inventions and post-employment restrictions
Once it is clear which rights are yours, agree a one-off payment for assigning them: a private deal, not a statutory inventor award

title: Seated with a senior leader at the Christmas party
situation: Your opener is well judged. The table warms up, they pick up the thread, and they ask in passing what you work on. It is a chance to be noticed, but it is only a passing question, time is short, and this is the wrong setting for a pitch.

options.text: Say in a couple of sentences what you do and why it matters, then stop without taking over the table
Treat it as a long status update, and sneak in a request while you are at it

title: In-house kernel versus an open-source stack
situation: Two months into the in-house build you are badly behind and keep missing milestones. At the quarterly review your manager puts you on the spot in front of everyone: 'This was your call. The business can't wait. Project X's core modules are already close to your design. Have a look at them, hit the milestone, and nobody's going to diff the code.' It is a way out, though not a clean one.

options.text: Quietly borrow the open-source kernel, rebrand it, and hit the milestone
Keep the work original, ask for a delay, and write the risk into the update

title: The company goes all-in on a new bet and sidelines your work
situation: The company loudly announces it is going all-in on a new technical direction. Headcount, budget and attention all move that way. The work you have spent years on is relabelled 'keep-the-lights-on' and starts to fade. People on the new project look like the future. People on the old product look like a question mark. You are free to say what you think of the technology. Do you try to move across?

options.text: Push for a place on the new work, start at the edges, and use what you know to catch up fast
Stay put on the old product and wait to see whether the new bet crashes
Spread a story you know is untrue, blame named people, and slow the new team's delivery
Write up the cost, how mature the technology is and the risk of migrating customers, then carry out the decision

title: Desk politics in the new office
situation: The first draft of the rules gets a fair hearing. A senior colleague tells you not to be naive: going by length of service would be simpler. The mood in the room turns tense.

options.text: Compromise: give length of service some weight, but keep rotation and type of work as the priorities
Stick to the original rules and push back on the senior colleague in public

title: Stuck on the ladder: move into management or go deeper?
situation: You neither move across nor go deeper. Your energy goes into complaining. While you stand still, you slide backwards: your technical skills stop moving, the management route never starts, and even the day job begins to sag.

options.text: Stop complaining, make a choice, and act on it
Stay stuck and keep blaming everyone else

title: Telling the client the project will be late
situation: You reported 'on time', then forced it through overnight. The version you shipped is rough and keeps failing once live. The client discovers that you hid the delay and delivered a poor product, and is beyond angry. You have ended up with the worst of both.

options.text: Tell the whole story, pull the broken version, and set a delivery plan that will actually hold
Keep patching it and play down how bad it was

title: The pay rise did not come through — coast in protest?
situation: Your request for a pay rise got nowhere this time. Your manager only said 'let's see'. You feel deflated, and your energy for the work drops. What next?

options.text: Hold your nerve, keep delivering, build your case for next time, and agree a date to revisit it
Protest by coasting and drag your feet on everything you can
In a huff, tell the whole office 'I'll walk', with no actual plan

title: A promotion without a pay rise
situation: You look at it coolly. If the title gives you real experience of leading people or owning a piece of work, and sets up the next pay and promotion conversation, it is worth having. If it is just a vague promise with extra work attached, you should be wary. You take that view into the conversation with your manager.

options.text: Take on the extra responsibility, but press for a clear pay-review date or the resources to match
Take the title and say nothing at all about money

title: Whether to tell your manager about a health problem
situation: You hide it and push through, and for a while the work gets done. Then, on a critical piece of work, you run out of steam, and people start to speculate.

options.text: Come clean now and adjust the plan
Keep hiding it and gamble that nobody notices

title: Your annual bonus falls short, and you go to your manager
situation: You go in hot. Your manager is left looking small, and the conversation turns into a clash of tempers. Even if you have a point, your manner puts them on the defensive about their authority, and they stop trying to help. Now the argument is about your temper.

options.text: Realise your manner was wrong, cool things down, and bring the conversation back to the facts
Get more heated, until neither of you will budge

title: One umbrella, a downpour, and Jordan at going-home time
situation: The umbrella is small and your shoulders still get wet. On the way Jordan talks about your manager squeezing the timetable lately, and they sound low. At the station they hesitate: “Want to grab a bowl of something hot near mine? On me.” The rain is getting heavier.

options.text: Accept, and listen to how the project is going
Decline and catch the last train home

title: Stay deep in the internals, or move to the application layer where results show faster?
situation: You face a choice of technical direction: keep digging into hard, slow internals that few people can do, or move towards the application layer, where results show faster and get more attention. Each path has a cost, and the choice will shape your technical standing later.

options.text: Weigh your strengths, interest, and long-term value, then make a clear-eyed choice
Chase quick wins and easier reviews, and follow the crowd into the application layer
Stay on internals out of snobbery, look down on the application layer, and ignore the practical return
